metadata.abstract_summary: CQRS splits a system's write side (Commands, a Domain-Driven-Design aggregate, a normalized transactional store) from its read side (Queries, a denormalized "Thin Read Layer" optimized to project DTOs directly) because a single conceptual model asked to serve both jobs well typically does neither — the split is motivated by data-model expressiveness, consistency requirements, and read/write load a

sections.heading: Claims
sections.text:
Young's own definition, given as the origin of the pattern:

> "Command and Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) originated with Bertrand Meyer's Command and Query Separation Principle... The fundamental difference is that in CQRS objects are split into two objects, one containing the Commands one containing the Queries."

And his own statement of why the split matters, given per-side rather than in terms of who may call which side:

> "Consistency — Command: It is far easier to process transactions with consistent data... Query: Most systems can be eventually consistent. Data Storage — Command: ...near 3rd Normal Form. Query: ...in a denormalized way... Scalability — Command: ...Scalability therefore is not always important. Query: ...Scalability is most often needed for the query side."

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Not an empirical study. This is a practitioner design document, explicitly described as having "originated as class manual" for teaching Domain-Driven-Design-adjacent architecture, structured as an incremental argument: start from a "Stereotypical Architecture" (a generic DTO-up/DTO-down CRUD system), show its problems, then apply CQRS and Event Sourcing as successive refinements, each illustrated with architecture diagrams and small worked code examples (a `CustomerService` split into `CustomerWriteService`/`CustomerReadService`).

sections.heading: Evidence & Limits
sections.text:
- **No empirical measurement anywhere in the document.** Every claim is argued from software-engineering first principles and the author's consulting experience, not benchmarked or tested. This is consistent with the document's own genre (a teaching document), but it means claims like "the CQRS and Event Sourcing model is actually less expensive in most cases" are asserted, not measured.
- **The operator-safety scenario this catalogue cares about is absent from the text.** The word "safety" does not appear in the context this gap analysis needs; every stated justification for separating Commands from Queries (Consistency, Data Storage, Scalability — see Claim) is about data-model shape and load, not about which caller is permitted to issue a mutating request.
- **The reference architecture itself contradicts a "display must never become a participant" reading.** Figure 26/27 in the source show one `Client` box sending both Commands (to the write side) and Queries (to the read side) through the same client. CQRS's own worked example is a client that legitimately does both — the pattern is silent on, and does not restrict, who or what may hold a reference to the Command side. A client that queries only would be a valid CQRS client, but nothing in the document says a client *may not* also send Commands; the split governs the *backend's* internal model boundary, not client-side authorization.
- **Undated within the document itself.** The PDF's own text carries no publication date; year 2010 is inferred from the hosting path (`/wp-content/uploads/2010/11/`) and from third-party attribution (search results consistently cite 2010), not confirmed from a dateline in the primary source.
